concepts.title: Why Services Aren't Enough for HTTP Routing
concepts.description: A Service operates at the packet level, rewriting destination IP and port, with no ability to read a Host header or a URL path, and provisioning a separate cloud load balancer per application doesn't scale operationally or financially. Both gaps motivate a dedicated, HTTP-aware entry point in front of many Services at once.
learningObjectives: Explain why a plain Service cannot route requests based on hostname or URL path, tying the explanation to how kube-proxy actually rewrites packets.
Explain the operational and financial cost of provisioning one LoadBalancer-type Service per externally-reachable application.
Distinguish Layer 4 (what a Service operates on) from Layer 7 (what HTTP-aware routing requires) in concrete terms.
Explain why centralizing TLS termination in one place is preferable to configuring certificates per Service.
Explain how these two gaps together motivate a single, shared, HTTP-aware entry point in front of multiple Services.

sections.heading: Recap: A Service Only Ever Sees IP and Port
sections.body:
As covered in the Services concept, kube-proxy implements a Service by programming packet-rewriting rules (historically iptables destination NAT, or IPVS and eBPF-based alternatives on some clusters) that rewrite a packet's destination from the Service's ClusterIP:port to a backing Pod's IP:targetPort. This works at Layer 4: it inspects and rewrites addressing information in the packet header and never parses the payload.

That matters the moment you want to say 'requests for api.example.com go to the api Service, and requests for app.example.com go to the web Service.' The hostname a browser sends (the `Host` header) lives inside the HTTP request, which is carried in the packet's payload, the part kube-proxy's rules never inspect. A Service's `spec` has no field for a hostname or a URL path, and that's not a missing feature waiting to be added: it follows from operating at a layer below where that information exists. The same goes for a path like `/orders` versus `/users`: both arrive in the HTTP request line, invisible to anything working with IP addresses and port numbers.

sections.heading: The Sprawl Problem: One Cloud Load Balancer Per Service
sections.body:
Recall from the Services concept that a `LoadBalancer`-type Service on a cloud provider provisions a managed external load balancer for that one Service. That works for a single application but doesn't scale as a pattern: ten HTTP applications that each need external access, each as its own `LoadBalancer` Service, means ten cloud load balancers, each with its own external IP, each billed hourly, and each needing its own DNS record and, for HTTPS, its own place to configure and rotate a TLS certificate.

This is a cost problem before it's an elegance problem: cloud load balancers aren't free, and ten running continuously cost noticeably more than one. It's also operational sprawl: ten surfaces where a certificate might expire unnoticed, ten DNS entries to keep straight, ten places a misconfiguration could hide. That gets worse as the number of exposed HTTP services grows into the dozens, which is ordinary beyond a small cluster.

sections.heading: What's Needed: HTTP-Aware Routing, in One Place
sections.body:
Written out, the requirement is about HTTP semantics: route on the `Host` header (`api.example.com` versus `app.example.com`), route on URL path prefix within a host (`/orders` to one backend, `/users` to another), and terminate TLS once, in one shared location, instead of configuring and rotating a certificate for every backend.

A Service can't express any of this, for the structural reason above. It requires something that terminates the HTTP connection and reads the request before deciding where it goes, which is a **Layer 7** concern (the application layer, where HTTP lives), not a Layer 4 one. What's needed is a single component in front of many backend Services doing request-aware routing, so that only *that component* needs an external IP, a load balancer, and a place to hold TLS certificates, and every Service behind it can stay a plain internal ClusterIP.

sections.heading: Before Ingress: The Reinvention People Try Anyway
sections.body:
It's worth naming the workaround people reach for before they learn about Ingress, because it has the shape of the solution Ingress formalizes: hand-roll a reverse proxy, typically an nginx or HAProxy Deployment with its own single `LoadBalancer` Service and a manually maintained config file mapping hostnames and paths to upstream ClusterIP Services. This works, and it solves the problem above (one external IP, one place for certs, HTTP-aware routing), but you write, deploy, and maintain that configuration by hand, outside Kubernetes' object model, with no standard way for other tooling to read or generate it.

Kubernetes' answer, covered in the next concept, standardizes this pattern into two pieces: the **Ingress** resource, a declarative object describing the desired routing rules (state, not a sequence of steps, like every other object so far), and an **Ingress controller**, a running component that watches those rules and implements them, typically as the kind of reverse-proxy Deployment just described, no longer hand-maintained.

examples.title: What a Service Spec Structurally Cannot Express
examples.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: api
spec:
  selector:
    app: api
  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 8080
  # There is no field anywhere in this spec for:
  #   - a hostname to match against (e.g. api.example.com)
  #   - a URL path to match against (e.g. /v2/orders)
  # Routing here is purely IP:port; nothing about HTTP is visible to this object.
examples.explanation: This is an ordinary, valid Service, and it's the full extent of what a Service can say about where traffic goes: a selector picking backing Pods, and a port mapping. Searching the Service API reference for a `host` or `path` field turns up nothing, because there is nothing; kube-proxy's packet rewriting couldn't consult such a field anyway, since it never parses the HTTP request the field would be compared against.

examples.title: Ten Apps, Ten Load Balancers
examples.code:
kubectl get svc -A -l expose=external
# NAMESPACE   NAME          TYPE           EXTERNAL-IP       PORT(S)
# team-a      checkout      LoadBalancer   203.0.113.10      80:31001/TCP
# team-a      catalog       LoadBalancer   203.0.113.11      80:31002/TCP
# team-b      accounts      LoadBalancer   203.0.113.12      80:31003/TCP
# team-b      notifications LoadBalancer   203.0.113.13      80:31004/TCP
# ...(6 more)...
examples.explanation: Each of these ten Services provisioned its own cloud-managed, billed load balancer with its own external IP: ten IPs to keep DNS pointed at, ten places to configure a TLS certificate for HTTPS, and ten times the baseline cost of an external load balancer, because each application asked for external access the most direct way it could. None of these Services can express host- or path-based routing, even if a team wanted to consolidate several apps under one domain. There's no field for it, only ten independent IP:port endpoints.

misconceptions.description: You can add multiple hostnames or paths to a single Service's spec to get host- or path-based routing, similar to how you can list multiple ports.
misconceptions.clarification: A Service spec has no field for hostname or URL path matching at any level. These aren't optional fields left unset; they don't exist in the Service API, because kube-proxy's packet rewriting never parses the HTTP payload where a Host header or request path lives. Routing by host or path needs something that terminates the HTTP connection and reads the request, a Layer 7 concern outside what a Service (a Layer 4 construct) can be extended to do.

misconceptions.description: Making an HTTP application reachable from outside the cluster always means giving it its own dedicated LoadBalancer-type Service.
misconceptions.clarification: It's possible, but it doesn't scale as a pattern: each LoadBalancer Service provisions its own billed, cloud-managed load balancer and external IP. The alternative, covered next, is to keep each application's Service internal (plain ClusterIP) and put a single shared, HTTP-aware entry point, an Ingress controller usually backed by one LoadBalancer Service of its own, in front of many of them, consolidating the external surface, the cost, and TLS certificate management in one place.

exercises.prompt: Given this Service, can it be configured to route example.com/api/* to this Service's Pods while example.com/web/* goes to a different Service, without introducing any additional Kubernetes object? Justify the answer by pointing to specifically what's missing.
exercises.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: api
spec:
  selector:
    app: api
  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 8080
hints: List every field this Service's spec actually has. Is there anywhere a URL path pattern could even be written?
Think about what kube-proxy would need to inspect to make a path-based decision, and whether it ever looks at that part of a packet at all.
The answer isn't 'this Service is misconfigured' -- it's that no configuration of a Service object, correct or otherwise, can express this.
exercises.expectedAnswer: No. This is not possible with a Service alone, however it's configured. A Service's spec has only a selector and a list of port mappings; there's no field for a URL path or hostname anywhere in the Service API. Path-based routing requires inspecting the HTTP request line inside the packet's payload, which kube-proxy's Layer 4 packet rewriting never does.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The Service API has no mechanism for this; it's not a matter of finding the right field, because the field doesn't exist. Every routing decision a Service makes is based on the destination IP:port a packet arrives with, rewritten by kube-proxy to a backing Pod's IP:targetPort, without parsing the packet's payload. A URL path like /api/orders lives inside the HTTP request line, which is payload, not addressing information, so no combination of Service fields could make this routing decision: a Service operates one layer below where paths and hostnames exist. This is the gap Ingress and an Ingress controller are built to fill.

exercises.prompt: A platform team provisioned 6 separate LoadBalancer Services (one per internal application) to give each app external HTTPS access, and now needs to renew and install a new wildcard TLS certificate for *.internal.example.com across the fleet before it expires. Diagnose why this rollout is unexpectedly slow and error-prone, and describe the structural fix (you don't need to write full Ingress YAML yet -- just identify the fix conceptually and show the 'before' state clearly).
exercises.code:
kubectl get svc -A -l tier=frontend -o wide
# NAMESPACE   NAME        TYPE           EXTERNAL-IP    PORT(S)
# team-a      orders      LoadBalancer   203.0.113.21   443:31101/TCP
# team-a      inventory   LoadBalancer   203.0.113.22   443:31102/TCP
# team-b      accounts    LoadBalancer   203.0.113.23   443:31103/TCP
# team-b      billing     LoadBalancer   203.0.113.24   443:31104/TCP
# team-c      search      LoadBalancer   203.0.113.25   443:31105/TCP
# team-c      reports     LoadBalancer   203.0.113.26   443:31106/TCP
# (TLS termination is configured independently, per Service, via each team's own proxy sidecar or cloud LB cert config)
hints: Count how many separate places the new certificate actually needs to be installed, and how many of those places are owned by different teams with different processes.
This isn't a Kubernetes bug to fix with a YAML change to any one of these Services -- it's a structural consequence of how many independent external entry points exist.
What single change in architecture would reduce 'six separate cert installs across three teams' down to one?
exercises.solutionExplanation: The slowness and error-proneness aren't caused by a misconfiguration in any one Service. They follow from having six independent external entry points, each with its own separately configured TLS termination, owned by three teams with three different (and possibly inconsistent) processes for installing a certificate. Renewing one wildcard cert means coordinating six changes in six places, any of which can be missed, misconfigured, or delayed relative to the others. That is the operational sprawl of a one-LoadBalancer-per-app pattern. The structural fix is to consolidate: convert these six Services to plain internal ClusterIP (removing their external IPs and LoadBalancer costs), and put a single Ingress controller, backed by one LoadBalancer Service, in front of all of them, with routing rules (covered in the next concept) sending each hostname or path to the right internal Service. The wildcard certificate is then installed and rotated in one place, however many internal applications sit behind it.

assessments.prompt: Which of the following is something a plain Kubernetes Service (ClusterIP, NodePort, or LoadBalancer) fundamentally cannot do, regardless of configuration?
options: Route incoming requests to different backends based on the HTTP Host header or URL path.
Load-balance traffic across multiple backing Pods.
Provide a stable virtual IP address that doesn't change as backing Pods are replaced.
Expose an application on a port in the 30000-32767 range on every node.
assessments.explanation: Host- and path-based routing requires parsing the HTTP request, a Layer 7 operation, which is outside what a Service does. A Service's mechanism (kube-proxy programming packet-rewriting rules) works on IP addresses and ports at Layer 4 and never inspects a packet's payload, so no configuration of any Service type adds this capability. The “Load-balance traffic across multiple backing Pods”, “Provide a stable virtual IP address…”, and “Expose an application on a port…” options are all things ordinary Services do provide (load-balancing across Ready backing Pods, a stable ClusterIP, and NodePort's node-level port), which is why they're not the answer to what a Service *cannot* do.

assessments.prompt: Before adopting Ingress, a team hand-rolls their own solution: an nginx Deployment with a manually maintained config file mapping hostnames to backend ClusterIP Services, fronted by its own single LoadBalancer Service. According to this concept, what is true about this workaround?
options: It doesn't actually solve the underlying problem -- Services still can't express host-based routing no matter what fronts them.
It's strictly worse than giving every application its own LoadBalancer Service, since it introduces a single point of failure with no compensating benefit.
It genuinely solves the same structural problem Ingress solves (one external IP, one place for certs, HTTP-aware routing).
It only works for path-based routing, never host-based routing, since nginx cannot inspect a Host header without a Kubernetes Ingress object present.
assessments.explanation: The hand-rolled proxy has the shape of the solution Ingress formalizes: it achieves one external IP, centralized TLS, and HTTP-aware routing, which is real progress over one-LoadBalancer-per-app. What it lacks is standardization: the routing configuration lives in a hand-maintained file outside any Kubernetes object, so nothing else in the ecosystem can read, generate, or reconcile it declaratively. The “It doesn't actually solve the underlying problem…” option is false: the workaround does solve the routing problem, just not in a standardized way. The “It's strictly worse than giving every application…” option ignores the benefits (consolidated IP, cert management) the workaround provides. The “It only works for path-based routing, never…” option is false: plain nginx, configured by hand, can inspect Host headers; that has nothing to do with whether a Kubernetes Ingress object exists.

assessments.prompt: According to this concept, what specifically is the cost of provisioning a separate LoadBalancer-type Service for each of ten independent HTTP applications, beyond simple repetition?
options: The cost is entirely offset, because every LoadBalancer Service in a cluster automatically shares one TLS certificate across all of them by default.
Only the DNS management cost actually multiplies; cloud load balancers themselves are provisioned free of charge regardless of how many are created.
It's purely aesthetic -- ten Services behave identically to one in terms of cost and operational risk, just with more YAML files to maintain.

Each LoadBalancer Service provisions its own separately-billed cloud load balancer and external IP, multiplying the ongoing cloud cost by roughly ten, and creates ten independent DNS records and ten independent places a TLS certificate could expire unnoticed -- an operational sprawl problem that worsens as the number of exposed applications grows.
assessments.explanation: The cost is a real one: each LoadBalancer Service is billed independently by the cloud provider, and beyond dollar cost, ten entry points means ten DNS records to keep straight and ten surfaces where a certificate might expire unnoticed, sprawl that compounds as the number of exposed apps grows into the dozens. The “It's purely aesthetic -- ten Services behave…” option dismisses a cost that is real and significant. The “Only the DNS management cost actually multiplies…” option is false: cloud load balancers aren't free. The “The cost is entirely offset, because every…” option invents certificate sharing that doesn't exist; each LoadBalancer Service's TLS configuration is independent.

assessments.prompt: Which pairing correctly matches each item to the network layer it actually operates at, per this concept's explanation of why a Service can't route by hostname or path?
options: The Layer 4 / Layer 7 distinction is a legacy networking term with no real bearing on what a Service can or cannot express.

Destination IP/port rewriting (what kube-proxy does) is a Layer 4 concern; the HTTP Host header and URL path (what host/path routing would require reading) are Layer 7 concerns, one level above anything kube-proxy ever inspects.
Both destination IP/port rewriting and HTTP header inspection happen at Layer 4; Layer 7 in Kubernetes refers only to TLS termination.
Destination IP/port rewriting is a Layer 7 concern; the HTTP Host header and URL path are Layer 4 concerns.
assessments.explanation: This is the structural reason a Service can't do host/path routing: kube-proxy operates on addressing information (IP, port) at Layer 4, while the HTTP request, including the Host header and URL path, lives inside the packet's payload at Layer 7, which kube-proxy's rewriting logic never parses. The “Destination IP/port rewriting is a Layer 7…” option reverses the two layers. The “Both destination IP/port rewriting and HTTP header…” option flattens the distinction, ignoring that HTTP is what defines Layer 7. The “The Layer 4 / Layer 7 distinction…” option dismisses the distinction that explains the whole gap Ingress exists to fill.

assessments.prompt: Explain, in terms of what information is available at each network layer, exactly why a Service cannot route HTTP requests by hostname or path, and describe the operational cost problem that arises from trying to work around this by giving every application its own LoadBalancer Service instead.
assessments.modelAnswer: A Service's routing, implemented by kube-proxy, operates at Layer 4: it programs rules that rewrite a packet's destination IP address and port from the Service's ClusterIP to a backing Pod's IP and targetPort, and that's all it inspects. The HTTP request, including the Host header identifying which domain the client intended and the URL path identifying the resource within it, exists inside the packet's payload, one layer up at Layer 7, and kube-proxy never parses it. A new field on the Service API couldn't fix this; it follows from the layer at which a Service's mechanism operates, which has no access to the information host/path routing needs. Given that gap, a natural workaround is to skip host/path routing and give every application its own externally reachable Service, typically type LoadBalancer, so each gets a dedicated entry point and no routing decision is needed. But this doesn't scale operationally: each LoadBalancer Service provisions its own cloud-managed load balancer, which means its own external IP to track in DNS, its own place to configure and rotate a TLS certificate if serving HTTPS, and its own ongoing hourly cost. Ten exposed applications means ten of everything (ten IPs, ten cert-rotation surfaces, ten cloud bills), and it multiplies as the number of externally reachable services grows. That sprawl motivates consolidating behind a single, shared, HTTP-aware entry point instead of provisioning one external load balancer per application.

concepts.title: Ingress and Ingress Controllers
concepts.description: An Ingress object is only a declared set of HTTP routing rules (host, path, backend, and optionally TLS) and does nothing on its own. A separate, running Ingress controller watches those rules and implements them as a reverse proxy, which is why an Ingress with no matching controller installed sits inert with an empty address forever.
learningObjectives: Explain the relationship between the Ingress resource (declared rules) and an Ingress controller (the running component that implements them), and predict what happens with no controller installed.
Write an Ingress rule that routes by host and by path to different backend Services.
Explain pathType (Exact vs Prefix vs ImplementationSpecific) and predict a routing outcome based on segment-aware prefix matching.
Explain how TLS termination works via an Ingress's tls block and a referenced Secret, and where decryption actually happens relative to the backend Pods.
Explain the purpose of IngressClass when more than one Ingress controller is installed in a cluster.
Debug an Ingress that returns 404/502 by tracing through controller presence, IngressClass, path matching, and backend Service/Endpoints.

sections.heading: The Ingress Resource: Declaring Routing Rules
sections.body:
An `Ingress` object declares routing rules: for a given host, and optionally a URL path prefix within that host, send matching requests to a specific backend Service and port:

```yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: storefront
spec:
  rules:
    - host: shop.example.com
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /orders
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: orders-svc
                port:
                  number: 80
          - path: /catalog
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: catalog-svc
                port:
                  number: 80
```

Like every other object so far, this is declarative: applying it persists a description of desired routing behavior in etcd. Applying this file doesn't change any proxy configuration anywhere by itself, which is the subject of the next section and the detail that trips people up the first time they use Ingress.

A note on the API's status: the Ingress API is stable but frozen, with no new features planned. Gateway API is its more expressive successor (richer routing, role-oriented resources), and the Kubernetes project now points new work toward it. Ingress remains widely deployed, so this module teaches it first. When an Ingress misbehaves, `kubectl describe ingress <name>` is the first stop: it lists each rule with the backend Service and its resolved endpoints, plus events from the controller. A rule can also use a wildcard host such as `*.example.com`, and a `defaultBackend` catches requests that match no rule.

sections.heading: The Ingress Controller: What Makes an Ingress Do Anything
sections.body:
Kubernetes core ships **no built-in Ingress controller**: the API server will accept, validate, and store an Ingress object even if nothing in the cluster is watching for it. An Ingress controller (Traefik, HAProxy Ingress, or a cloud provider's own, such as the AWS Load Balancer Controller or GKE's Ingress controller; ingress-nginx was long the default choice, but the Kubernetes project retired it in March 2026, so existing installs no longer receive fixes) is a separate component you install deliberately, and it's what watches Ingress objects and implements the rules they declare.

Mechanically, most Ingress controllers are an ordinary Deployment of reverse-proxy Pods (commonly nginx or Envoy underneath), fronted by **one** `LoadBalancer`-type Service. That's how the sprawl problem from the previous concept collapses: instead of one cloud load balancer per application there's one, in front of the controller, and every application's Service can go back to being a plain, internal ClusterIP. The controller watches Ingress, Service, and EndpointSlice objects, regenerates its proxy configuration (an `nginx.conf`, for nginx-based controllers) to match the declared rules, and reloads it, automatically and in reaction to changes, the same watch-and-reconcile shape as every controller covered since the Control Plane concept.

The common failure mode this explains: applying an Ingress in a cluster with no controller (or none configured to watch it, covered under IngressClass below) leaves `kubectl get ingress` showing a permanently blank `ADDRESS`, and no request ever reaches any backend, not because the YAML is wrong but because nothing is implementing it.

sections.heading: pathType: Segment-Aware Matching, Not Raw String Prefixes
sections.body:
`pathType: Exact` requires the request path to match the declared path exactly, with no trailing segments. `pathType: Prefix` matches the declared path and any deeper path *segments* beneath it, but matching is **element-wise on `/`-separated segments**, not a naive string prefix comparison. A rule for `path: /orders` with `pathType: Prefix` matches `/orders`, `/orders/123`, and `/orders/123/items`, but **not** `/ordersarchive`: `ordersarchive` is a different path segment from `orders`, even though `/orders` is a character-for-character prefix of `/ordersarchive`.

```yaml
spec:
  rules:
    - http:
        paths:
          - path: /orders
            pathType: Prefix   # matches /orders, /orders/123 -- NOT /ordersarchive
```

`pathType: ImplementationSpecific` defers interpretation to whatever the installed controller does with the path string. Some controllers (ingress-nginx, via annotations) layer regex matching on top of this mode, which is powerful but means matching behavior isn't portable across controllers, unlike Exact and Prefix, whose semantics are part of the Kubernetes API regardless of which controller implements them.

sections.heading: TLS Termination at the Edge
sections.body:
An Ingress's `tls` block names one or more hosts and a Secret (of type `kubernetes.io/tls`, holding a certificate and private key) to use for HTTPS on those hosts:

```yaml
spec:
  tls:
    - hosts:
        - shop.example.com
      secretName: shop-tls-cert
  rules:
    - host: shop.example.com
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: storefront-svc
                port:
                  number: 80
```

The Ingress controller terminates TLS at that single edge: it decrypts the incoming HTTPS connection using the referenced certificate and, by default, forwards the request to the matched backend Service as **plain HTTP** over the cluster's internal network. This is the centralization the previous concept was building toward: backend Pods and Services generally need no certificate configuration at all, and rotating a certificate means updating one Secret referenced by the Ingress, not touching every backend. Tools such as cert-manager can issue and renew that Secret automatically. (Some controllers can re-encrypt the connection to the backend for defense in depth, via annotations, but plain HTTP to the backend over the cluster's internal network is the default and by far the most common setup.)

sections.heading: IngressClass: Choosing Which Controller Owns Which Ingress
sections.body:
A cluster can run more than one Ingress controller at once, for example an internal-facing Traefik instance for services that should never leave the private network alongside an external-facing controller for public traffic. `IngressClass` is the object that names a controller implementation, and an Ingress's `spec.ingressClassName` field says which one should implement its rules:

```yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: storefront
spec:
  ingressClassName: nginx-external
  rules:
    - host: shop.example.com
      ...
```

Most controllers are configured to watch only Ingress objects naming their own class (or, if marked as the cluster's default IngressClass, Ingress objects that omit the field). That allows a subtler variant of the 'nothing is implementing this' failure: an Ingress that names a class no controller claims (a typo, or a class for a controller since uninstalled) sits as inert as one in a cluster with no controller, even though `kubectl get ingress` and the object itself look unremarkable. The mismatch only shows up when you compare `kubectl get ingressclass` against the Ingress's `ingressClassName`.

examples.title: Host- and Path-Based Routing to Two Different Backends
examples.code:
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: storefront
spec:
  ingressClassName: nginx-external
  rules:
    - host: shop.example.com
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /orders
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: orders-svc
                port:
                  number: 80
          - path: /
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: storefront-svc
                port:
                  number: 80
examples.explanation: A request for `shop.example.com/orders/42` matches the first rule (its path segments start with `orders`) and goes to `orders-svc`; a request for `shop.example.com/about` doesn't match `/orders` at the segment level, falls through to the catch-all `path: /` rule, and lands on `storefront-svc`. Both rules resolve to plain ClusterIP Services: neither `orders-svc` nor `storefront-svc` needs an external IP or LoadBalancer, and the Ingress controller is the only component with an external-facing address in this setup.

examples.title: TLS Termination, Traced End to End
examples.code:
kubectl create secret tls shop-tls-cert \
  --cert=shop.example.com.crt --key=shop.example.com.key

curl -v https://shop.example.com/orders/42
# * (TLS handshake lines omitted; the handshake is with the Ingress controller)
# * using HTTP/1.1
# > GET /orders/42 HTTP/1.1
# > Host: shop.example.com
# < HTTP/1.1 200 OK

# Inside the cluster, the controller's own logs show the backend call as plain HTTP:
kubectl logs -n ingress-nginx deploy/ingress-nginx-controller | tail -1
# 10.244.3.12 - [shop.example.com] "GET /orders/42 HTTP/1.1" 200 ... upstream: "http://10.244.1.9:80/orders/42"
examples.explanation: The client's `curl` sees an ordinary HTTPS response; from its point of view the TLS handshake ends at whatever IP `shop.example.com` resolves to, which is the Ingress controller's LoadBalancer Service. The controller's log line shows the *upstream* call to the backend Pod as plain `http://`, not `https://`, confirming that decryption happened once, at the controller, and the request continued as unencrypted HTTP across the cluster's internal network.

examples.title: Diagnosing an Ingress That Never Gets an Address
examples.code:
kubectl get ingress storefront
# NAME         CLASS   HOSTS               ADDRESS   PORTS   AGE
# storefront   nginx   shop.example.com              80,443  14m
# ^ ADDRESS has been blank for 14 minutes -- something is missing

kubectl get ingressclass
# NAME            CONTROLLER
# nginx-external  k8s.io/ingress-nginx

# storefront's spec says ingressClassName: nginx -- but the real IngressClass is 'nginx-external'
examples.explanation: The `CLASS` column shows `nginx`, but `kubectl get ingressclass` shows the installed class is `nginx-external`: a naming mismatch, almost certainly a typo when the Ingress was written. Because no installed controller claims the class `nginx`, nothing is watching this Ingress, which is why `ADDRESS` has stayed blank well past when it should have populated. The fix is to correct `ingressClassName` to match the real IngressClass, not to investigate the controller's health or the backend Services, which are likely fine.

misconceptions.description: Applying an Ingress resource is sufficient, on its own, to make an application reachable via HTTP from outside the cluster -- the same way applying a LoadBalancer Service is.
misconceptions.clarification: An Ingress is a declared set of routing rules persisted as an object, and Kubernetes core ships no built-in controller that implements it. Without a separately installed Ingress controller watching that Ingress (and, in a multi-controller cluster, a matching IngressClass), the object does nothing: no proxy is configured, no load balancer exists because of it, and `kubectl get ingress` shows a permanently blank ADDRESS. A LoadBalancer Service, by contrast, is implemented by the cloud-controller-manager as a built-in part of the platform, which is why it doesn't have this 'nothing is watching it' failure mode.
misconceptions.fact: An Ingress is a declared set of routing rules persisted as an object, and Kubernetes core ships no built-in controller that implements it.

misconceptions.description: pathType: Prefix does a plain string-prefix comparison, so a rule for path /orders would also match a request to /ordersarchive.
misconceptions.clarification: Prefix matching in the Ingress API is path-segment aware: it splits both the rule's path and the request's path on `/` and compares segment by segment. /orders matches /orders and /orders/123 but not /ordersarchive, because ordersarchive is a different, single path segment, even though the raw string /orders is a literal prefix of /ordersarchive. Treating pathType: Prefix as naive string-prefix matching is a common and surprising mistake the first time someone hits it.

exercises.prompt: An Ingress has exactly one rule: host api.example.com, path /v1, pathType: Prefix, backend v1-svc. A client requests https://api.example.com/v1beta/users. Does this request match the rule and get routed to v1-svc, or not -- and why specifically?
exercises.code:
spec:
  rules:
    - host: api.example.com
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /v1
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: v1-svc
                port:
                  number: 80
hints: pathType: Prefix compares path SEGMENTS split on '/', not raw characters -- write out the segments of /v1 and of /v1beta/users separately.
Is 'v1beta' the same path segment as 'v1', or a different one, even though it starts with the same characters?
If nothing matches, what would a client actually receive back from the Ingress controller -- a route to the wrong backend, or a 404?
exercises.expectedAnswer: It does NOT match, and the request is not routed to v1-svc. /v1beta/users has a first path segment of 'v1beta', which is a distinct segment from 'v1' -- Prefix matching requires the full segment to match, not just a shared character prefix. With no other rule to fall back to, the client would receive a 404 from the Ingress controller itself, not a response from v1-svc.
exercises.solutionExplanation: pathType: Prefix splits both the declared path and the incoming request path into segments on '/' and requires the declared segments to match a full, leading run of the request's segments; it is not a raw string.startswith() comparison. /v1 has one segment, 'v1'; the request /v1beta/users has a first segment of 'v1beta', a different string, not 'v1' with something appended. Because 'v1' != 'v1beta' as whole segments, the rule doesn't match, even though the text /v1 is a character-for-character prefix of /v1beta. With no other rule to catch this path, the Ingress controller has nothing to route it to and returns its own 404, so v1-svc's Pods never see the request and play no part in the failure.

exercises.prompt: An Ingress and a backend Service both look correct, but every request returns a 502 Bad Gateway from the Ingress controller. `kubectl get endpoints checkout-svc` shows no addresses. Find and fix the bug (the bug is in the Service, not the Ingress).
exercises.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: checkout-svc
spec:
  selector:
    app: checkout-app
  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 8080
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: checkout
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: checkout
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: checkout
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: checkout
          image: checkout:2.0
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8080
hints: A 502 from an Ingress controller almost always means the controller successfully matched a rule but couldn't reach any actual backend Pod -- which points at the Service layer, not the Ingress rule itself.
Compare the Service's selector value, character for character, against the label the Deployment actually stamps on its Pods.
This is exactly the same class of bug covered in the Services concept -- an empty Endpoints object always means the selector matched zero Pods.
exercises.solutionCode:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: checkout-svc
spec:
  selector:
    app: checkout
  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 8080
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: checkout
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: checkout
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: checkout
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: checkout
          image: checkout:2.0
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8080
exercises.solutionExplanation: checkout-svc's selector is app: checkout-app, but the Deployment's Pod template stamps app: checkout (no '-app' suffix) onto its Pods. The match is exact and case-sensitive, so the Service matches zero Pods, as kubectl get endpoints checkout-svc confirms. The Ingress controller did its job: it matched the request to the right rule and tried to forward it to checkout-svc, but found no ready backend behind that Service. The exact status code for that depends on the controller: some return 503 when a Service has no endpoints (ingress-nginx does), while others, such as cloud load-balancer based ones, return 502. Either way the failure is downstream of the routing decision. Correcting the selector to app: checkout fixes the label match, populates the Endpoints object with the two checkout Pods, and clears the error with no change to the Ingress object. Fixing a selector needs no restart of the controller or the Pods: the Endpoints update is picked up automatically.

assessments.prompt: A team applies a syntactically valid Ingress object in a brand-new cluster that has never had any Ingress-related component installed. What is the most likely observed result?
options: The Ingress works immediately -- Kubernetes includes a built-in default Ingress controller that activates automatically whenever an Ingress object is created.
kubectl get ingress shows the object with a permanently blank ADDRESS, and no request from any client ever reaches any backend through it.
The API server rejects the Ingress at apply time with an error, since Ingress objects require a controller to be installed first as a precondition of validation.
The Ingress automatically falls back to behaving like a plain ClusterIP Service for each backend named in its rules.
assessments.explanation: Kubernetes core ships no built-in Ingress controller. The API server stores a valid Ingress object with nobody watching it, which is why ADDRESS stays blank indefinitely and no traffic is routed. The “The Ingress works immediately -- Kubernetes includes…” option is false: no default controller is bundled with the platform. The “The API server rejects the Ingress…” option is false: validation of an Ingress object's shape has nothing to do with whether a controller is installed, and the apply succeeds regardless. The “The Ingress automatically falls back to behaving…” option describes a fallback that doesn't exist: an unimplemented Ingress does nothing.

assessments.prompt: An Ingress rule uses `path: /orders` with `pathType: Exact`. Which of these requests actually matches this rule?
options: Neither matches anything unless an accompanying regex annotation is also configured on the Ingress.
Only /orders/123 matches, since Exact always requires at least one trailing path segment beyond the literally declared path.
Only /orders matches; /orders/123 does not, because Exact permits no additional trailing segments at all, unlike Prefix.
Both /orders and /orders/123 match, since Exact still permits deeper path segments beneath the declared path, similar to Prefix.
assessments.explanation: pathType: Exact requires the request path to match the declared path exactly, with no additional trailing segments; that's the difference from Prefix, which allows deeper segments beneath the declared path. The “Both /orders and /orders/123 match, since Exact…” option describes Prefix's behavior, not Exact's. The “Neither matches anything unless an accompanying regex…” option invents a dependency on regex annotations that Exact matching doesn't need. The “Only /orders/123 matches, since Exact always requires…” option inverts the relationship: Exact matches the bare declared path, not a path with a mandatory suffix.

assessments.prompt: A client gets a 404 directly from the Ingress controller (not from any backend application) for a request whose host/path combination no Ingress rule declares at all. What does this specifically indicate, compared to what a 502 for a different request would indicate?
options: A 404 here means the controller itself found no Ingress rule matching the request's host/path.
Both status codes are interchangeable in an Ingress controller and can represent any routing failure equally.
A 404 here means the controller found a matching rule but the backend Service had no Ready Pods; a 502 would mean no rule matched at all.
A 404 always originates from the backend application itself, having received the request but found no matching route of its own.
assessments.explanation: This maps onto where in the routing chain the failure occurred: a 404 from the controller itself is a routing-rule failure, since nothing in the Ingress's declared rules matched the request and no backend was consulted. A 5xx such as 502 or 503, by contrast, means the controller's routing succeeded (a rule matched, a Service was selected) but reaching a healthy Pod behind that Service failed, as in this concept's debugging exercise, where an empty Endpoints object produced a 5xx although the Ingress rule was correct. The “A 404 here means the controller found…” option swaps the two meanings. The “Both status codes are interchangeable…” option ignores that these codes signal different failure points. The “A 404 always originates from the backend…” option is wrong here: the backend is never reached when the Ingress controller itself returns the 404.

assessments.prompt: A cluster runs one healthy, correctly installed Ingress controller watching IngressClass `nginx-external`. A new Ingress object is applied with `ingressClassName: nginx` -- a typo; no IngressClass named exactly `nginx` exists. What is the most likely observed symptom?
options: The API server rejects the Ingress object outright at apply time, since ingressClassName must reference an existing IngressClass to pass schema validation.
The controller automatically renames the typo'd class to the closest matching real IngressClass name via fuzzy string matching.
The controller treats any unrecognized class name as its own default and implements the rules anyway, logging only a warning.
The Ingress sits inert -- ADDRESS stays blank and no traffic is ever routed through it.
assessments.explanation: Most controllers only watch Ingress objects naming their own class, so a class name that matches nothing real means nothing claims this Ingress, even while the same controller correctly serves every other Ingress in the cluster. Nothing about the Ingress object or the controller's health looks wrong in isolation; the mismatch only shows when you cross-check ingressClassName against kubectl get ingressclass. The “The controller treats any unrecognized class name…” option invents fallback behavior most controllers don't implement. The “The API server rejects the Ingress object…” option is false: the API server doesn't validate that ingressClassName references an existing object at apply time. The “The controller automatically renames the typo'd class…” option invents a fuzzy-matching feature that doesn't exist.

assessments.prompt: Trace, in order, exactly what happens to an HTTPS request for https://shop.example.com/orders/42 from the moment it reaches the cluster to the moment a specific backend Pod handles it, naming every component involved and what each one is responsible for.
assessments.modelAnswer: The client resolves shop.example.com to the external IP of the Ingress controller's own front-facing LoadBalancer Service, not to any IP belonging to orders-svc or its Pods, which remain internal-only ClusterIP Services. TLS is terminated at the Ingress controller, which uses the certificate and key in the Secret referenced by the Ingress's tls block to decrypt the request; from there on, the request is plain HTTP as far as anything inside the cluster is concerned. The controller reads the decrypted request's Host header (shop.example.com) and path (/orders/42) and compares them against the routing rules of every Ingress it watches that names its IngressClass (or the cluster default), finding the rule for host shop.example.com with a Prefix match on /orders, which names orders-svc as the backend. The controller then picks one of that Service's Ready backing Pods from its EndpointSlices and forwards the request as plain HTTP to that Pod's IP and targetPort. (Most controllers do this themselves and bypass kube-proxy, as the upstream Pod IP in the log example shows; a controller that sends to the Service's ClusterIP instead relies on kube-proxy's Layer 4 rewrite from the Services concept to choose the Pod.) That Pod handles the request, and the response travels back the same way in reverse to the Ingress controller, which returns it over the client's HTTPS connection, encrypted. Each component does one narrow job: the Ingress controller reads HTTP and picks a backend Service, and the Service's EndpointSlices say which Pods are eligible and Ready. Removing either host/path routing or the Service abstraction would leave a gap the other doesn't cover.

concepts.title: Kubernetes DNS: How Service Names Resolve
concepts.description: The stable Service names used in every earlier concept resolve to current IP addresses via CoreDNS, a cluster addon that watches the same Service and EndpointSlice objects every other controller watches. Knowing what a lookup returns for a normal Service versus a headless one is what makes per-Pod addressing in StatefulSets, and cross-namespace lookups, predictable.
learningObjectives: Explain what CoreDNS is and how it stays in sync with live cluster state, rather than serving from a static configuration file.
Construct a Service's fully qualified DNS name from its name, namespace, and cluster domain, and explain why a bare short name also resolves from within the same namespace.
Explain what an A record for a normal ClusterIP Service resolves to, versus what the same kind of lookup against a headless Service returns.
Explain how per-Pod DNS records for a StatefulSet differ from what an ordinary Deployment-managed Pod gets.
Debug a cross-namespace DNS resolution failure caused by relying on a short name instead of a fully-qualified one.

sections.heading: CoreDNS: A Watching Controller, Not a Static Zone File
sections.body:
Cluster DNS is provided by **CoreDNS**, which runs as an ordinary Deployment (typically named `coredns`, in the `kube-system` namespace) fronted by its own ClusterIP Service. The kubelet populates every Pod's `/etc/resolv.conf` by default (`dnsPolicy: ClusterFirst`) to send DNS queries to that Service's IP, so DNS inside the cluster is another Service-fronted application, with nothing exotic underneath.

```bash
kubectl exec app-pod -- cat /etc/resolv.conf
# nameserver 10.96.0.10
# search default.svc.cluster.local svc.cluster.local cluster.local
# options ndots:5
```

CoreDNS runs the `kubernetes` plugin, which watches the API server for Service and EndpointSlice changes (the same watch-and-react shape as every controller since the Control Plane concept) and answers DNS queries from that live state. There is no hand-maintained zone file: create a new Service and it becomes resolvable as soon as CoreDNS's watch notices the change, typically within seconds, with no DNS administration step.

sections.heading: The FQDN Pattern and Why Short Names Work
sections.body:
A Service's fully qualified DNS name follows the pattern `<service-name>.<namespace>.svc.<cluster-domain>`: `web.default.svc.cluster.local` for a Service named `web` in the `default` namespace, on a cluster using the very common default cluster domain `cluster.local`.

CoreDNS doesn't special-case a bare name like `web`. What makes `nslookup web` work from a Pod in the same namespace is the `search` list in that Pod's `resolv.conf`, shown above: `default.svc.cluster.local`, `svc.cluster.local`, `cluster.local`, in that order. The resolver in the Pod's container tries appending each suffix in turn until one resolves: `web` becomes `web.default.svc.cluster.local` on the first attempt, which succeeds, so the search stops. This is ordinary Unix resolver behavior; Kubernetes' contribution is populating that search list per Pod, scoped to the Pod's own namespace.

A Pod in a *different* namespace trying the same bare `web` would have its own namespace's suffix tried first, and would only resolve the intended Service by including at least the namespace, `web.other-namespace`, which lets the search list fill in `.svc.cluster.local`, or by using the fully qualified name.

One side effect is worth knowing. The `options ndots:5` line tells the resolver to try the search list first for any name with fewer than five dots, so a lookup of an external name like `api.example.com` (two dots) first tries `api.example.com.default.svc.cluster.local` and the other suffixes, each a wasted query, before the bare name. Ending the name with a trailing dot (`api.example.com.`) marks it fully qualified and skips the search list.

sections.heading: What the Record Returns: ClusterIP vs. Headless
sections.body:
For a normal Service (one with a ClusterIP), an A record lookup of its DNS name returns one address: the Service's stable ClusterIP, the virtual address kube-proxy already has rewrite rules for. DNS's job is narrow: translate a name to that one virtual IP. The load-balancing across the Pods backing the Service happens afterward, at the packet-rewriting layer, not in DNS.

```bash
kubectl exec app-pod -- nslookup web
# Name:   web.default.svc.cluster.local
# Address: 10.96.14.201     <-- the Service's ClusterIP, one address, every time
```

A **headless** Service (`clusterIP: None`) has no virtual IP for DNS to return, so CoreDNS returns a set of A records, one per currently **Ready** backing Pod, each resolving to that Pod's own IP:

```bash
kubectl exec app-pod -- nslookup web-headless
# Name:   web-headless.default.svc.cluster.local
# Address: 10.244.1.14
# Address: 10.244.2.31
# Address: 10.244.3.8
```

Here DNS itself is the discovery mechanism: a client resolving `web-headless` gets the current member list, with no kube-proxy rewriting involved, since there's no virtual IP to rewrite.

sections.heading: Per-Pod DNS: The Mechanism Behind StatefulSet Identity
sections.body:
As introduced in the StatefulSets concept, pairing a StatefulSet with a headless governing Service gives each Pod its **own** additional DNS record of the form `<pod-name>.<service-name>.<namespace>.svc.<cluster-domain>` (`web-0.web.default.svc.cluster.local`), resolving only to that Pod's IP, however many other Pods share the headless Service.

```bash
kubectl exec app-pod -- nslookup web-0.web
# Name:   web-0.web.default.svc.cluster.local
# Address: 10.244.1.14     <-- specifically web-0's IP, not any other replica's
```

This is the mechanism, not just a naming convention, that lets a peer address 'replica 0' rather than 'any interchangeable member of the pool.' An ordinary Deployment-managed Pod has **no individual DNS record of its own** under any Service configuration. Only the Service in front of a Deployment's Pods is addressable by name, because those Pods have no stable per-replica identity for a record to attach to. (Clusters can also resolve IP-derived names such as `10-244-1-14.default.pod.cluster.local`, but those change whenever the Pod's IP does, so they aren't an identity.)

sections.heading: The Common Bug: Namespace-Relative Search Order
sections.body:
The most common real-world DNS bug isn't a broken CoreDNS; it's a bare short name used from the wrong namespace. If a Pod in namespace `frontend` looks up `api`, and `frontend` *also* contains a Service named `api` (unrelated to the `api` Service the caller meant, which lives in `backend`), the search list resolves `api.frontend.svc.cluster.local` first, successfully, and stops. The caller reaches the *wrong* Service with no error, no warning, and no sign at the DNS level that anything went wrong, because the search order found *a* match before it tried the intended one.

The reliable fix is to be as explicit as the situation requires: use at least `<service>.<namespace>` for any cross-namespace reference (the search list fills in `.svc.cluster.local`), or the fully qualified name, instead of a bare short name whose resolution depends on what else exists in the caller's namespace. That can change under a working configuration if a same-named Service is added locally later.

examples.title: resolv.conf and a Basic Service Lookup
examples.code:
kubectl exec app-pod -- cat /etc/resolv.conf
# nameserver 10.96.0.10
# search default.svc.cluster.local svc.cluster.local cluster.local
# options ndots:5

kubectl exec app-pod -- nslookup web
# Name:   web.default.svc.cluster.local
# Address: 10.96.14.201

kubectl exec app-pod -- nslookup web.default.svc.cluster.local
# Name:   web.default.svc.cluster.local
# Address: 10.96.14.201
examples.explanation: Both lookups resolve to the same address, 10.96.14.201, web's stable ClusterIP, because the search list appends the same default.svc.cluster.local suffix to the bare name `web` that the fully qualified query already spells out. CoreDNS doesn't treat the two queries differently; the search list is a client-side convenience that saves typing the full name, applied by the resolver before the query reaches the nameserver at 10.96.0.10.

examples.title: Headless Service DNS: All Pod IPs, or One Specific Pod
examples.code:
kubectl exec app-pod -- nslookup web-headless
# Address: 10.244.1.14
# Address: 10.244.2.31
# Address: 10.244.3.8

kubectl exec app-pod -- nslookup web-1.web-headless
# Address: 10.244.2.31     <-- specifically web-1's own IP, one address only
examples.explanation: The first query, against the headless Service's own name with no Pod prefix, returns every currently Ready backing Pod's IP as a separate A record; there's no virtual IP to return instead. The second query, prefixed with the Pod's name (web-1.), narrows that to one address: that Pod's own IP. This is the mechanism a StatefulSet peer uses to address 'web-1' rather than receiving the entire unordered member list and having to guess.

examples.title: A Silent Wrong-Namespace Match
examples.code:
# Pod is running in namespace 'frontend'
kubectl exec frontend-pod -n frontend -- nslookup api
# Name:   api.frontend.svc.cluster.local
# Address: 10.96.30.5      <-- resolved to frontend's OWN 'api' Service

# The intended target was actually in a different namespace:
kubectl get svc api -n backend -o jsonpath='{.spec.clusterIP}'
# 10.96.44.19               <-- a different IP; never reached
examples.explanation: There's no error anywhere in this trace. `nslookup api` succeeds on the first search-suffix attempt, because namespace frontend also contains a Service named api, unrelated to the intended backend api Service. The request goes to the wrong destination with no DNS-level signal; only comparing the resolved IP against the intended Service's ClusterIP reveals the mismatch. That's why relying on bare short names for cross-namespace references is fragile: correctness depends on whether a same-named Service exists locally, which can change independently of the code doing the lookup.

misconceptions.description: Every Pod gets its own DNS name automatically, the same basic way every Service does.
misconceptions.clarification: Only Services get a DNS name by default. An ordinary Deployment-managed Pod has no stable DNS record of its own; only the Service in front of it is addressable by name. The exception is a StatefulSet Pod paired with a headless governing Service, which also gets its own per-Pod record, because that pairing is how StatefulSets provide stable, addressable per-replica identity. It's a deliberate, narrow feature of that combination, not a general property of Pods.

misconceptions.description: A Service's DNS name always resolves to one IP, with load-balancing across replicas happening somewhere inside DNS itself.
misconceptions.clarification: That's true only for a normal (non-headless) Service, where DNS resolves to one stable ClusterIP and the load-balancing across backing Pods happens afterward, at the kube-proxy packet-rewriting layer; DNS never sees or chooses between individual Pods. A headless Service inverts this: there's no ClusterIP to return, so DNS hands back every backing Pod's IP, and any load-balancing or member selection happens client-side from that list. In that case DNS, not kube-proxy, is the discovery mechanism.

exercises.prompt: Namespace backend contains a Service named api (ClusterIP 10.96.44.19), intended for cluster-wide use. Namespace frontend also happens to contain an unrelated Service also named api (ClusterIP 10.96.30.5), created independently by a different team for their own purposes. A Pod running in namespace frontend runs `nslookup api`. Which address does it get back, and what does this reveal about relying on bare short names?
exercises.code:
kubectl exec somepod -n frontend -- nslookup api
# Address: ?
hints: Check the Pod's own resolv.conf search list -- which namespace's suffix does it try appending FIRST?
The search stops at the first suffix that resolves successfully -- does it ever get to try the OTHER namespace's api Service at all?
This isn't a broken or slow DNS lookup -- it succeeds immediately. The problem is which Service it succeeds against.
exercises.expectedAnswer: It resolves to 10.96.30.5, frontend's own unrelated api Service, not the intended backend one. The Pod's resolv.conf search list tries frontend.svc.cluster.local first (since the Pod itself is in namespace frontend), that attempt succeeds immediately against the local api Service, and the search stops there without ever trying anything in namespace backend.
exercises.solutionExplanation: Resolution of a bare short name is relative to the namespace of the Pod doing the lookup, via that Pod's resolv.conf search list, which tries the calling Pod's own namespace suffix first. Since frontend contains a Service named api, the lookup succeeds on the first attempt (api.frontend.svc.cluster.local), and the resolver has no reason to try another suffix, so it never considers backend's api Service. The caller silently talks to the wrong Service, with a successful, error-free DNS resolution throughout. That's why any cross-namespace reference should use at least api.backend (letting the search list fill in the rest) or the fully qualified name, instead of a bare short name whose meaning depends on what else exists in the caller's namespace.

exercises.prompt: A StatefulSet-backed cache cluster is paired with a headless Service, web-headless. An application is supposed to always write to the current primary replica specifically, web-0, but it currently connects using the plain headless Service name and gets a different, effectively random replica's IP on different runs. Identify the bug and the correct hostname to use instead.
exercises.code:
# Application connection string, currently:
CACHE_HOST=web-headless.default.svc.cluster.local

# Observed: different runs of the app connect to different replica IPs,
# sometimes web-0, sometimes web-1, sometimes web-2; never reliably the primary.
hints: What does resolving the plain headless Service name actually return -- one address, or a set of addresses covering every current replica?
If multiple addresses come back, which one a given client library picks first (or at random) is not something this hostname lets you control at all.
There's a specific, different DNS name format -- covered in this concept -- for addressing exactly one named replica, rather than 'the whole headless Service.'
exercises.solutionCode:
# Correct connection string: addresses web-0 SPECIFICALLY, not the whole pool:
CACHE_HOST=web-0.web-headless.default.svc.cluster.local
exercises.solutionExplanation: Resolving web-headless.default.svc.cluster.local (the headless Service's own name, with no Pod prefix) returns an A record for every currently Ready backing Pod, web-0, web-1, and web-2 at once, and which one a DNS client or connection library uses first is effectively arbitrary from the application's perspective, which explains the inconsistency. The fix is the per-Pod DNS name, prefixing the Pod's name onto the headless Service's name: web-0.web-headless.default.svc.cluster.local resolves to one address, web-0's own IP, regardless of how many other replicas exist or what state they're in. This is what StatefulSets pair with headless Services to enable: addressing one named replica deterministically instead of an unordered pool.

assessments.prompt: What does an A record lookup of a normal (non-headless) Service's DNS name return, compared to the same kind of lookup against a headless Service?
options: Neither returns anything useful without also querying an accompanying SRV record first.
A normal Service returns a list of backing Pod IPs for the client to choose from; a headless Service returns just one aggregate virtual IP.
Both return the same thing -- a single virtual IP -- since all Services, headless or not, are assigned a ClusterIP by Kubernetes.
A normal Service returns its one stable ClusterIP; a headless Service, having no ClusterIP at all, returns a set of A records.
assessments.explanation: This is the reverse of a common intuition: a normal Service resolves to one stable virtual IP (its ClusterIP), with the spreading of traffic across replicas handled later by kube-proxy, not DNS. A headless Service (clusterIP: None) has no virtual IP to return, so CoreDNS returns the individual IPs of every currently Ready backing Pod, making DNS the discovery mechanism in that case. The “Both return the same thing…” option is false because headless Services are defined by NOT having a ClusterIP. The “A normal Service returns a list…” option swaps the two behaviors. The “Neither returns anything useful without also querying…” option invents a dependency on SRV records that doesn't exist for basic A-record resolution.

assessments.prompt: A Deployment-managed Pod named `web-7d9f8c9b7-4x2lp` runs behind a ClusterIP Service named `web`. Does this specific Pod have its own individual DNS record that another Pod could look up directly?
options: No, but only because this Pod's name contains a randomly generated hash suffix; a Deployment using a fixed, non-random Pod name would get one.
No -- an ordinary Deployment-managed Pod has no individual DNS record of its own under any Service configuration.
Yes, but only because this specific Pod's name happens to be longer than the Service's own name.
Yes -- every Pod behind any Service automatically receives a per-Pod DNS record of this form, the same way a StatefulSet Pod does.
assessments.explanation: Per-Pod DNS comes specifically from the StatefulSet-plus-headless-Service combination, not from anything a Pod gets automatically. A Deployment-managed Pod, whatever its name, has no individual DNS record under any Service configuration; clients can only address the Service in front of it. The “Yes -- every Pod behind any Service…” option overgeneralizes a StatefulSet-specific feature to all Pods. The “Yes, but only because this specific Pod's…” option invents a rule about name length. The “No, but only because this Pod's name…” option is wrong: the random suffix has nothing to do with whether a Pod gets a DNS record; the determining factor is the StatefulSet-plus-headless pairing.

assessments.prompt: Per this concept, what is the most reliable way to reference a Service that lives in a different namespace than the calling Pod, given that a bare short name's resolution depends entirely on the calling Pod's own namespace search order?
options: Set ndots:1 in the calling Pod's own resolv.conf, which forces every lookup to be treated as already fully qualified regardless of namespace.
Always use the bare short name -- CoreDNS automatically searches every namespace in the cluster until it finds a uniquely matching Service.

Use at least `<service-name>.<namespace>` (letting the search list fill in the remaining .svc.cluster.local suffix), or the fully qualified name outright -- rather than depending on a bare short name whose resolution is contingent on whatever else happens to exist in the caller's own namespace.
Rename the Service in the target namespace so that no other namespace in the cluster could ever contain a same-named Service.
assessments.explanation: The fix is to use at least <service>.<namespace>, or the fully qualified name, instead of a bare short name. A bare short name is resolved through the calling Pod's own search list, which tries the caller's own namespace first, so cross-namespace bare-name lookups are fragile in the way this concept's example shows. The “Always use the bare short name…” option is false: CoreDNS doesn't search every namespace; only the suffixes in the calling Pod's search list are tried, in order, stopping at the first success. The “Set ndots:1 in the calling Pod's own…” option misapplies ndots, which controls whether a name is treated as already fully qualified based on dot count, not namespace scoping. The “Rename the Service in the target namespace…” option is impractical and doesn't scale as organizational policy.

assessments.prompt: A new Service is created in the cluster. Roughly how soon does it become resolvable via CoreDNS, and why?
options: Typically within seconds, with no manual administration step at all -- CoreDNS's kubernetes plugin watches the API server for Service and Endpoints/EndpointSlice changes and answers queries from that continuously updated, in-memory view, rather than from any static zone file.
Only after CoreDNS's next scheduled resync, which per this concept defaults to once every 24 hours.
Immediately and unconditionally, because CoreDNS pre-generates DNS records for every possible future Service name in advance.
It requires a manual DNS zone file update and a CoreDNS restart, similar to traditional on-premises DNS administration.
assessments.explanation: CoreDNS's kubernetes plugin follows the same watch-and-react shape as every other controller covered here: it watches Service and EndpointSlice objects and answers from that live state, with no static zone file and no DNS administration step. The “It requires a manual DNS zone file…” option describes traditional DNS administration, the opposite of this design. The “Immediately and unconditionally, because CoreDNS pre-generates DNS…” option invents a pre-generation mechanism that doesn't exist and couldn't (Kubernetes can't enumerate 'every possible future Service name'). The “Only after CoreDNS's next scheduled resync…” option invents a 24-hour resync interval that this concept never states.

assessments.prompt: Explain the full mechanism by which a Pod's DNS query for a Service name actually gets answered, from the Pod's own configuration through to CoreDNS's own data source, and explain why this makes Service DNS 'eventually consistent with cluster state' rather than a static configuration.
assessments.modelAnswer: When a Pod issues a DNS query, whether for a bare short name or a fully qualified one, it goes to the nameserver in the Pod's /etc/resolv.conf, which the kubelet populates by default to point at CoreDNS's ClusterIP (an ordinary Service, reached through the same Service networking covered earlier). If a bare short name was used, the Pod's resolver first tries appending each suffix from the resolv.conf search list in order, the calling Pod's own namespace suffix first, until one query succeeds, which is why a short name's resolution is relative to the namespace the calling Pod lives in. When the now fully qualified query reaches CoreDNS, its kubernetes plugin answers without consulting any static zone file: it holds an in-memory view of cluster Service and EndpointSlice objects, kept synchronized by watching the API server, the same watch mechanism every other controller uses. For a normal Service, the plugin answers from the Service object's ClusterIP; for a headless Service, from the current list of Ready addresses in its EndpointSlices, since there's no ClusterIP to return. This watch-based design is why Service DNS is eventually consistent with cluster state instead of static: a new Service, or a Pod becoming Ready or unready behind a headless Service, appears in DNS answers within however long CoreDNS's watch takes to notice and its response cache (if configured) takes to expire, typically seconds, with no zone file edit or reload by a human.
